newsitem.title: UK: Nickel, steel scrap still plentiful in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Nickel, steel scrap still plentiful in Europe.

text.p: Supplies of Russian nickel and stainless steel scrap are still plentiful in Western Europe, physical traders said.
And although orders books have picked up slightly, the stock overhang could delay a strong pick up in the physical market until well into 1997, they added.
"There is still a lot of primary nickel around," said one.
"There are indications that order books are picking up and getting a little better. But there is also a lot of Russian nickel easily available as before," a major producer added.
Traders and merchants said Russian material was arriving in the region, being cut and put into LME warehouses, partly explaining the rising trend in inventories.
Some smaller traders were also said to have cut and delivered off-market stocks of Russian material into the LME (London Metal Exchange) to avoid financing the metal.
"I know of two companies who over the holidays thought it better just to cut and deliver metal in at discounts from $100 to $120 (a tonne) rather than finance it," said one merchant.
But bigger players who had financing in place were more likely to hold on to the material, another merchant added.
"The bigger players who have the financing in place will probably not," he said. "Financing costs and the contango are basically the same, so there is no real cost," he added.
Spot discounts for Russian uncut nickel to LME cash weakened to $80-$130 a tonne from $50-$100 around five weeks ago.
"There is material still coming out of Russia without doubt, and in order to shift it people are offering bigger discounts," a trader said.
As well as the Russian overhang, high stocks of stainless steel scrap were also depressing the market.
"(Stainless) stocks are still very high. The world market has been in oversupply by some 500,000 tonnes this year, and this is still not completely consumed," said a scrap trader.
Nickel-in-scrap as a ratio of LME cash was quoted at around 90 percent, although one nickel dealer said he traded as high as 94 percent. This compares with 88/91 percent in mid-September.
Scrap traders said the stocks were slowly being drawn down, but did not see a dramatic rise in prices until mid-1997.
The big stainless steel mills were still preferring to take in a high scrap ratio while it remained at cheap levels.
But smaller foundries were less flexible, and were taking bigger tonnages of LME nickel for blending, traders said.
"We have seen small spot purchases from customers all over Europe," said a merchant. "So the spot market has picked up, but not in a huge way."
He and other traders agreed it would be some time before the Russian/scrap overhang was worked down to more normal levels.
"I think you've got to rule out this year for a recovery in terms of the physical market. I would see a stronger pick-up in the first or second quarter of next year," he said.
"I firmly believe that primary business will not be anything special until the second half of next year," another added.
Melting premiums were quoted at six to 10 cents a pound ($132 to $220/tonne) from five to eight cents in mid-September.
Plating premiums were also slightly steadier at around 15 cents ($331) from 10 to 15 cents five weeks ago.
